newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Southern African, EU ministers to meet on trade.
newsitem.headline: Southern African, EU ministers to meet on trade.

text.p: Foreign ministers from 12 southern African states meet their European Union counterparts for two days starting on Monday to look for ways to boost trade and investment between them.

Southern African Development Community (SADC) executive secretary Kaire Mbuende said the Namibia meeting would also address the region's political concerns, along with global problems ranging from Burundi to Bosnia.
Most community members appeared cautious about a U.S.- proposed all-African intervention force of around 10,000 troops that could be deployed in times of crisis, Mbuende told Reuters.
He said more emphasis was needed on preventing conflicts.

"We have not (yet) discussed the issue...but the general consensus appears to be that this should be an African initiative and even then, we need to look at whether we are not developing too militaristic solutions," he said.
"There is a danger of the world casting Africa simply in a military role. We must also be seen as an intellectual force."

Mbuende said the SADC was eager to ensure European Union support for the peace efforts in Angola and to end the crisis in Burundi -- a former Belgian protectorate -- where military strongman Pierre Buyoya seized power in July.
"In these cases there is room for some EU members such as Belgium and France to use their political influence," he said.
The conference also aims to boost programmes to fight problems such as drug trafficking.
Mbuende said the ministers would spend time looking at the future of trade relations between southern Africa and Europe, particularly after the Lome Convention expires in the year 2000.
The convention, agreed in 1975, is the biggest aid and trade pact linking the EU to mostly former European colonies in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.
The ministers would also address the dispute between South Africa and the EU on a free trade agreement.
Europe has offered a deal that excludes major agricultural products from South Africa, which has angered the Pretoria government.
But other members of the SADC and the Southern African Customs Union have demanded assurances that any deal between South Africa and the EU would not prejudice them.
The SADC comprises Angola, Botswana, Malawi, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Lesotho, South Africa, Swaziland, Tanzania, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
